#10328. Three Qualities That Can Make You an Inspiring Leader

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Imagine you’re on a plane and suddenly hear an explosion. The whole plane rattles, and you see the left engine is on fire. After another loud noise, you realize there’s a hole in the side of the aircraft. As air rushes out, the plane is rapidly descending—over 20,000 feet in less than five minutes.

If you faced what passengers of Southwest Airlines 1380 experienced, you would probably do what they did: frantically write goodbye messages to your family and loved ones, thinking that these are your last moments on Earth.

But on that flight, the pilot, Captain Tammie Jo Shults, came on the intercom and said 10 simple words: “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.”

The passengers would later talk about how those 10 words were transformative, turning their panic into possibility. By sharing those 10 words, Captain Shults was helping her passengers make sense of their experience and reframe the dramatic descent, from “plummeting to Earth” to a planned and orchestrated path to safety.

As Captain Shults expertly landed the plane, she calmly and peacefully talked to air traffic control. After landing, she got up and went row by row, looking every passenger in the eye to make sure they were OK. People talked afterward about her words, her stature, and her empathy as she walked down that aisle.

Contrast Captain Shults’s experience with another captain who also dealt with a massive hole in his vessel, Francesco Schettino, captain of the Costa Concordia. Headed out on a seven-day cruise in the Mediterranean, the ship got too close to shore. It’s debatable why that happened: Captain Schettino claims he was saluting mariners on the shore; prosecutors claim he was trying to impress his mistress who was on board. But what isn’t in dispute is what happened next: The rocks tore a 115-foot hole in the side of the ship, which caused it to eventually capsize.

Before calling the Coast Guard, Captain Schettino spent time getting his story straight. The crash had caused an electrical blackout, but he was going to try to say that the blackout caused the crash. He tried to pin the responsibility on the helmsman. It took him almost an hour after the crash to sound the evacuation siren.

While people were frantically trying to find safety, Captain Schettino was nowhere to be found. Finally, the Coast Guard discovered him in a lifeboat—though Captain Schettino claimed that he “accidentally” fell into the lifeboat. But he also somehow fell out of his captain’s uniform. He was sitting in a lifeboat watching his boat sinking, hiding in civilian clothing. You can hear the outrage in the Coast Guard’s voice when he says in an audio recording, “I’m gonna make you pay for this.” And Captain Schettino did pay. He was sentenced to 12 years in prison for manslaughter and abandoning ship.

These two people faced very similar situations. They were both captains, dealing with holes in the side of their vessels, but how they responded to their crises was completely different. Captain Shults helped people make sense of their experience. She was courageous, competent, and calm in landing the plane, and she compassionately connected to each of her passengers. In contrast, Captain Schettino caused the accident, refused to take any responsibility, and did not take any action to help his passengers save their lives. As a result of his selfish negligence, 32 people died, and numerous people were injured.

Why do some leaders create feelings of inspiration that percolate a wellspring of hope and possibility in others, while other leaders create seething cauldrons of infuriation and resentment? I’ve asked this question to tens of thousands of people across the globe, and here is what I learned about what makes a leader inspiring.

My first big idea is that “inspiring” and “infuriating” leaders exist on an enduring continuum that is made up of three universal factors:

We can inspire people in how we communicate, how we present ourselves, and how we interact with others—through our words, our actions, and our interactions.

My second big idea is that these are the three factors of inspiring leadership because each one fulfills a fundamental human need. Being visionary fulfills the fundamental need for meaning and understanding. That’s what Captain Shults provided when she said, “We’re not going down; we’re going to Philly.” She helped people make sense of their experience.

Being an exemplar fulfills the fundamental need for protection and passion. Captain Shults courageously protected her passengers with her calm and competence.

And being a mentor fulfills the fundamental human need for belonging and status. That’s what Captain Shults offered as she walked down the aisle: She made her passengers feel recognized and seen.

By surveying tens of thousands of people across the globe, I have found these three dimensions to be universal. There is not a single inspiring characteristic that is mentioned in one country that’s not mentioned in the dozens of countries in the world where I have collected data.

Effective visionaries not only offer a clear perspective on the world, but they also make their vision easy to follow and understand, and so engaging that it captures our attention.

The easiest way to make something easy is to make it simple. I call this the Inception Rule, after the movie Inception, where Leonardo DiCaprio tries to plant an idea in someone’s head during a dream. He discovers it’s not about how deep you go; it’s about how simple the idea is. As a leader, you want to constantly be thinking how to reduce your ideas to their simple core.

Another way that we can make things easy to understand is to repeat them, the way a chorus repeats in a song. The more people hear it, the more they will remember it.

Let’s consider Zoom’s vision: Delivering Happiness. It’s simple, and bubbly. But that vision is also deeply practical—it helped Zoom’s employees efficiently make high-stakes decisions during the chaos of the COVID-19 pandemic. As millions of people began using the product for the first time, Zoom needed to decide on its product’s baseline level of functionality. Too many features would overwhelm people, but too few features would stymie people. They needed the Goldilocks baseline of features to deliver happiness.

Similarly, delivering happiness led Zoom to invest heavily in customer service. Most of us know how much an hour-long wait for customer service can destroy happiness. So, Zoom hired many agents so wait times would be as short as possible.

To make our visions more engaging, we can use visual language. Andrew Carton, an associate professor of management at Wharton, did a study where people were told that a company’s mission was to either “make our customers satisfied” or “make our customers smile.” Then, he had people create a product. When they were working under the more visual vision (“smile”), they created more engaging products.

How to become more visionary: We can inspire people to be more visionary by having them reflect on their values. In one of my studies, we worked with a Swiss employment agency. When people came in to register for benefits, half of them were asked to reflect on their values, why those values mattered to them, and how they demonstrated them. For example, my own values include generosity, courage, and kaizen (a Japanese word for continued improvement).

Two months later, the people who had reflected on their values were twice as likely to have a job. The effects were so profound that the employment agency asked us to end our study and give everyone the reflection activity.

To be a great exemplar, the first thing you want to do is to consistently embody your vision; don’t be a hypocrite. As former CEO of PepsiCo Indra Nooyi once noted, “Don’t ask someone to do something that you wouldn’t do [yourself].”

Inspiring exemplars are calm and courageous protectors, like Captain Shults. And they show passion. When you ask someone to talk about a passion of theirs, their eyes light up, they smile a big beaming smile, they speak quickly and dramatically use their hands, and they lean in as if telling you a secret. When we are passionate about something, it’s revealed in our eyes, our mouth, our voice, and our bodies. And when you listen to someone’s passion, you smile, your eyes light up, and you feel the energy inside of you.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series

In my research on Dragon’s Den, which is a variant of Shark Tank, when entrepreneurs expressed more passion—in their eyes, their voice, their hands—they were dramatically more likely to receive funding. You can’t inspire others if you aren’t inspired.

How to become a better exemplar: Think about the moments in your life when you felt the most powerful and in control, your best self. Hundreds of studies around the world have used this technique that my colleagues Deb Gruenfeld, Joe Magee, and I created. We’ve even found that people are more likely to be selected for jobs if they’ve engaged in this reflection.

Consider this proverb by Confucius: “Tell me and I will forget, show me and I may remember, involve me and I will understand.” When you involve people, they feel seen and heard and they feel like people, not objects.

Inspiring leaders empower others everywhere across the globe. Even in cultures that are less individualistic than the United States—like Thailand or Saudi Arabia—there’s nothing more infuriating than when a boss micromanages you, rather than involves you or trusts you.

Inspiring leaders also elevate others. They share credit rather than steal credit, which is one of the most infuriating things that can happen at work. Finally, inspiring leaders empathize with others. They do what Captain Shults did, in making sure each of her passengers were OK, versus only thinking about themselves, like Captain Schettino.

How to become a better mentor: Reflect on the perspectives of others. My colleagues and I did a study with medical students who were tasked with diagnosing what was wrong with patients. Before meeting their patients, half the students were told to take the perspectives of their patients and to think about a recent time when they had engaged in perspective taking. Ultimately, the patients were more satisfied, trusting, and likely to follow the advice of the doctor who had been reminded to engage in perspective taking.

My third big idea is that inspiring leaders aren’t just born; they’re also made. Because there is a universal set of inspiring attributes and behaviors, they can be practiced, nurtured, and developed.

My fourth big idea is that when you’re a leader, you don’t have the option of not having an impact. Your behavior is going to inspire or infuriate. I call this the “leader amplification effect.” Everything you say and do as a leader gets amplified. Your criticisms become humiliating criticisms, but your compliments become glorious praise.

My fifth big idea is that you can REIP what you sow. This phrase, drawn from the Bible, suggests that if we put inspiring energy out in the world, we receive inspiring energy in return. But my REIP is a homonym of reap, and it stands for reflect, emulate, intend, and practice:

My final big idea is that inspiring leaders think like architects. Like an architect who designs buildings to produce particular reactions and interactions, leaders design policies and practices that lead people down the inspiring path, even when they’re not present. So instead of just changing individual behavior, you can think about: How can you change a broader dynamic?

Thinking like an architect moves you from viewing a situation as a person problem—What’s wrong with this employee?—to start to think about what’s wrong in their environment, and how you can redesign that environment to help the employee be the best version of themselves.

Here’s one practice that Joseph Stagliano, president of NBT Bank, designed to inspire those around him. Although he has over 1,200 employees, he sends a birthday greeting to every single person. That sounds impossible, but he does it in 10 to 15 minutes over coffee every day.

The message is simple yet personalized. He showed me an example that said, “Hey Monica [pseudonym], Happy birthday! I hope you had a great weekend? How did track and bowling go?” Although his message was short, Monica’s response was extensive, overflowing with information and enthusiasm.

I shared that idea with the CEO of another company, and then a month later, he told me he started doing something similar. Every morning over coffee, he reached out to one person in his organization, and he expressed either gratitude or praise. He said he did this to put a skip in their step, but they ended up sending him such glowing replies that it put a skip in his step. The CEO reaped the inspiring energy he sowed. You can, too.

This essay is based on a talk that is part of the Positive Links Speaker Series by the University of Michigan’s Center for Positive Organizations. The Center is dedicated to building a better world by pioneering the science of thriving organizations.

Adam Galinsky is a professor at the Columbia Business School. He is author or co-author of more than 200 scientific articles, the bestselling book INSPIRE: The Universal Path for Leading Yourself and Others (HarperCollins, 2025), the bestselling book Friend & Foe (Penguin Random House, 2015), and a popular TED talk, How to Speak Up for Yourself, with over 7.8 million views.

Generous parental leave policies improve health for moms and babies, family finances, and equality at work and at home.

Try these Greater Good in Action practices to build appreciation, trust, and kindness in your workplace.

Hunter‑gatherer societies are often put on a pedestal for being truly egalitarian—but the reality is more complicated.

Does your organization elicit gratitude--or make people feel taken for granted?

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

Psychologist and meditation teacher Tara Brach explores how practicing kindness and compassion can strengthen our relationships, ease loneliness, and help us feel more connected to others.

#10325. Chinese web giant Tencent says new US GPU ban ‘sets everyone back in China’

Don’t hoist the Mission Accomplished banner, because company president thinks it also will spur China’s chip biz into action

The USA’s new ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent.

Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Lau said the new US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business.

“It does set everyone back. It sets everyone back in China,” Lau said. “So everyone is actually having less advanced compute to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China.”

He said the ban will impact Tencent’s ability to train models.

“Our training efficiency with Hy4 is actually very high,” he said. “When we look at the next version, it would take probably longer time for us to come up with the next version in the short run.”

“But over time, the domestic supply chain would actually come on board.”

Lau also thinks the bans won’t hamper Tencent’s ability to run inferencing workloads, because made-in-China chips “should be able to cover it.”

“And over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we see the industry is progressing very fast,” he added. “With the latest restriction, we expect it to actually speed up even further, because all the development effort would actually have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.”

Tencent needs GPUs, and lots of them, because the 10 million users of its agentic assistant WorkBuddy are collectively consuming over 100 trillion tokens per day. Lau thinks WorkBuddy is on track to becoming a hit product, partly because many users are outside China.

Lau said Tencent can serve WorkBuddy customers outside China because the service can operate with different models, and the company thinks it can find third parties to provide the necessary inferencing services without the new US bans creating a problem.

But Lau said that GPU rentals and other cloud services, which are also growing strongly, may be impacted.

“In terms of cloud, if it is non-GPU related, we can actually build capacities ourselves outside of China,” he said. “I think there is still a lot of such opportunities because our cloud service is actually very cost competitive. When it comes to GPU, then unfortunately, we cannot actually offer high-end GPU anymore. We may be able to work with some partners in different places.”

Tencent doesn’t break out revenue for its cloud services, but said they rose by 35 percent year-on-year, well ahead of the company’s overall eight percent growth. Marketing services also grew strongly, by 19 percent, thanks in part to new AI-powered systems that improve ad targeting.

The company’s WeChat and Weixin messaging platforms continued to grow, adding 35 million accounts to exiting the quarter with 1.44 billion monthly active users.

One Tencent biz that went backwards was its international gaming unit, which saw revenue fall nine percent.

Chief strategy officer James Mitchell said that slowdown wasn’t caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. “I think that in fairness, the slowdown for us predated the run-up to GTA VI,” he said, before predicting that Tencent’s existing and future “evergreen games” should help to turn things around.

“The game environment globally is one where the rate of innovation has slowed somewhat, and now with AI, there’s opportunities to re-accelerate innovation,” he said. ®

#10322. AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

First, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console shows the new capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

Next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview shows what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

That’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

For production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab shows the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

Serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

See GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10320. Four Ways to Help Newcomers Feel Like They Belong

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Liz Cahill was born and raised in Philadelphia. Her whole family is from Philadelphia, going back generations. One day, she was offered an internship in the Bay Area and decided to make the leap, despite not knowing anything about it or anyone there.

“I said goodbye to everything I knew and loved in Philadelphia and came to the Bay. Not knowing a soul.”

When she arrived, it hit her. “I was like, wow, I’m in a place that like, literally nobody knows me. So if I am dead in a ditch, like nobody will figure it out for a long time.”

This could have been a story of loneliness and disconnection, but it wasn’t, because someone took her under their wings—actually two strangers, her roommates Lauren and Deirdre. “They took me in and welcomed me and brought me into their whole social world, which showed me so much love.”

This isn’t the experience for most people. Darilys Matos Acevedo grew up in Puerto Rico. “In Puerto Rico, a stranger talks to you all the time. If you went down the street and you talked to somebody, if you made eye contact . . . you had to smile at them or you said good morning or good afternoon.”

Then she moved to Boston for graduate school. “I had never even visited the place. I knew nobody here.” And where she got smiles and small talk in Puerto Rico, in Boston she “got glares.” “And I’m like, oh, OK. You don’t do any of that here.” It was painful and created a large void in her life.

As Darilys talked to other Latinos in Boston, she assumed “I’m the only one who feels this way, but I wasn’t. There was like a whole group of people that felt like that.”

Their stories are different, but they reveal the same truth.

Moving doesn’t simply change where we live. It interrupts the invisible web of relationships that makes everyday life feel familiar, that makes us feel like we belong. And the majority of the 13 million American adults who move each year experience this.

At the US Chamber of Connection, our recent study on social connection in America explored the impact of life transitions on social connection. It found that 40% of people navigating a relocation struggle with social connection, and they report 35% more barriers to connection compared to everyone else. Two of the most common barriers are not knowing where to start and not wanting to go out alone.

The impact is lasting, as someone shared with us. “Two years ago, I was going on a vacation, and I could not find ONE neighbor to water my plants while I was away. I had lived in this building on and off for over 15 years. I was mortified. How could it be that I had nobody in my building to help with such a small task?”

Moving ranks among the most stressful life events a person can experience, on par with divorce and job loss. But the stress isn’t just logistical; it’s psychological. Moving severs the informal ties and daily routines that quietly anchor our sense of who we are and where we belong. The result is a predictable but rarely named experience: not just loneliness, but identity dislocation. The question isn’t only “who do I know here?” but “who am I here?”

This month, we're teaming up with the US Chamber of Connection for Welcome Week. Together, we're mobilizing communities, neighborhoods, and organizations nationwide to do one simple thing this September: open the door to a new friend. Make a pledge to invite someone in and help us reach our goal to make 100,000 people feel welcomed!

To understand the scale of that loss, consider what a typical adult social network requires to build: roughly 200 hours to develop a close friend, 90 hours for a friend, and five hours of repeated interaction for each of the weak ties (neighbors, familiar faces, community contacts) that make daily life feel anchored. A typical adult carries around 1,300 hours of accumulated relationship time. When you move, you leave all of it behind and start from zero.

This is also, paradoxically, what makes the first year after a move one of the most powerful windows for connection. Disruption breaks old habits and makes people unusually open to forming new ones, a phenomenon researchers call the habit discontinuity effect. People who have just moved are more likely to join things, try things, and reach out than they were six months earlier at home.

What closes that window isn’t lack of desire. Research by Nicholas Epley at the University of Chicago finds that people systematically underestimate how much strangers want to connect and overestimate how awkward the attempt will be. Both the newcomer and the potential neighbor hold back, each assuming the other isn’t interested. Both tend to be wrong.

And the effects of getting it right last longer than most people expect. Vanessa Elias, the founder of Block Party USA, shared with us the story of a neighbor who brought her family a pie when she moved in as a six year old. She remembers her name, Mrs. Fisher, decades later.

What would happen if welcoming became a civic practice instead of an individual virtue? This year, the US Chamber of Connection recruited over 250 people across 25 states to run creative experiments that aimed to help others feel more welcome in their neighborhoods. They were trained on the science of connection and worked together across the country to support each other. We call them the Welcome Committee.

For many of the volunteers, they signed up because they had an experience like Liz. One shared that “when we arrived to our new town we felt welcomed, surprised, and alive through these touches, and wanted to build more.” Or as another volunteer explained, “people are still welcoming me and I still feel at home here. So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I wanna create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”

For others, it came from an experience more akin to Darilys’s. “I would have loved to find this kind of thing when I moved,” shared one early volunteer. “I’ve been in my neighborhood and city since 2019 and have yet to make close friends in the neighborhood or city where I live. It feels scary and uncomfortable to get out there. But I’m realizing the huge impact of not having close friends. I’m ready to make the effort. Because if I’m feeling this way, I can’t be the only one.”

They each began by inviting a neighbor for a conversation. They shared their stories of their neighborhoods growing up. Dreamed about the ideal neighborhood together. Explored the Six Points of Connection, a clear and actionable checklist for individuals and leaders to define and strengthen social bonds. And then they explored how they might together make the neighborhood more connected.

They ran some creative experiments. Lindsay turned their suburban garage door into a community message board. Kaitlin created a traveling tin of homemade baked goods that moves neighbor to neighbor down the street, each recipient required to bake something and pass it on to someone new. Sarah hosted a gathering for other people named Sara(h) in her town. Courtney started flyering the neighborhood to organize a dog gathering in someone’s backyard. Nithya left a flower and a handwritten note for each of the five nearest neighbors inviting them to coffee.

Many of the volunteers nostalgically tried things they remembered from their childhood or had seen in a movie. Kate moved an iron chair and table to her front step and started having her morning coffee there facing the street. Jon made lemonade with his kids and set out donuts for anyone walking by. Chet started introducing himself on his daily dog walks. Anne organized a multi-household yard sale across eight houses. And many of them hosted potlucks and block parties.

They all expressed knowing “how meaningful it can be to walk into a new space and find someone who is genuinely glad you are there.” And they wanted to make people feel that way.

As the volunteers conducted their experiments, they began to share their findings. They mirrored much of what we have learned from social scientists over the last 50 years. Four themes emerged that help to inform how we can all do more to help new residents, and any neighbor, feel more welcomed.

1. The first step is the most important. Stop playing “invite chicken.” Many of our volunteers shared a version of the same experience: sitting at home hoping someone would call and invite them to hang out, attend an event, or even just watch Netflix together. They assumed that the people they wanted to call were probably busy or uninterested. Those people were likely sitting at home thinking the same thing. Nobody called. Everyone stayed alone.

Call it invite chicken: a standoff where everyone loses despite everyone wanting the same thing. The barrier isn’t reality; it’s anticipation. Someone just has to go first.

And sometimes, when we do break the game of chicken, we don’t get the response we wanted. When Hazel hosted her first neighborhood coffee gathering, one neighbor texted that he was too nervous to come. She didn’t give up. She texted back encouraging him. He came. At one of Elizabeth’s gatherings in San Diego, a man had been dragged along by his wife, who promised they’d stay just five minutes. He was the last to leave.

We are poor forecasters of our own social experiences. People overweight the discomfort of initiation and underweight the pleasure of connection. The host who sends the follow-up text, the wife who insists on five minutes, isn’t being pushy. They’re correcting for a cognitive error the reluctant person can’t see from the inside.

2. We are more motivated working together. Partner with someone. Erin hosted a neighborhood gathering in New York City and reflected afterward on what she’d do differently. Her top lesson: “I appreciated the help I did get from neighbors and wished I’d had a co-planner to share more of the work with.”

This is consistent with what research finds: People are significantly more likely to initiate and sustain kind and helpful behavior when they’re doing it alongside someone else. A partner doesn’t just make the work easier; they make follow-through more likely, because the social cost of backing out now involves someone else. Several Welcome Committee volunteers named the US Chamber of Connection cohort itself as the thing that got them out the door. Not the training, not the tools, but the fact that others were doing it, too.

3. We gain comfort with repeat exposure. Build a rhythm. Hansen has been hosting a monthly porch gathering (coffee, bagels, same spot) for two years. Recently, he watched neighbors spontaneously make plans to go cycling together and quietly organize to look out for a boy on the street whose father is dying of cancer. Neither of those things was planned. They happened because the same people had been attending his events and they had built comfort with each other. Hansen didn’t suggest they help the boy but had created the environment for it to be possible.

Research finds that repeated contact with the same faces makes us like and trust them more, independent of what’s said. Those repeated encounters build weak ties, which are how people find help in a crisis, how trust spreads beyond close friends, how a community starts to look out for itself. The first gathering gets you in the door. Showing up again is what builds the neighborhood.

What these moments share is spontaneity and clarity of intent. Research finds that unexpected gestures create a positive disruption that formal invitations don’t. They bypass the social calculation people run when a stranger approaches, and they signal warmth without asking for anything back. Research finds that being noticed is the precondition for feeling like you belong.

And having a clear role removes the ambiguity that makes first moves feel risky. When Annie said “I’m a Welcome Committee member,” her motives were transparent before she said another word. You don’t need a plan. You need to look up.

Giving to others produces more sustained well-being than spending on yourself. The helper’s high is real. Welcoming a newcomer isn’t just a form of service; it’s one of the highest-return social investments you can make.

Liz knows this firsthand. The woman who arrived in the Bay Area not knowing a soul, wondering if anyone would notice if she disappeared, is now the person who creates spaces for others to land. “People here took a chance on me,” she says. “So it gave me this strong sense of duty to pay that forward. I want to create spaces where people can land and feel comfortable.”

All friendships begin the same way: by talking to strangers. Someone just has to go first. Years later, Liz became the person who notices.

Aaron Hurst is a pioneer social entrepreneur and CEO focused on rebuilding human connection to strengthen communities. He founded the U.S. Chamber of Connection to address the national decline in social ties and trust. Previously, he founded the Taproot Foundation, sparking a $15B pro bono service movement, and led Imperative, which developed purpose profiling tools used by over 200 companies. He’s also co-founder of Board.Dev, connecting tech leaders to nonprofit boards. Author of The Purpose Economy, Aaron’s work has shaped the purpose movement in business and been featured in The New York Times, Bloomberg, and SSIR. He lives in Seattle with his family.

Couples who embrace their own “microculture”—pet names, inside jokes, and rituals—may be happier and more satisfied with their relationship.

Sending reels on social media may seem frivolous or distracting, but it actually functions as a form of relationship maintenance.

New research is exploring how our brains translate other people's actions into the experience of feeling loved.

Do you embrace a diversity of backgrounds and opinions in others?

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

Psychologist and meditation teacher Tara Brach explores how practicing kindness and compassion can strengthen our relationships, ease loneliness, and help us feel more connected to others.

#10319. South Korea tries to out exam cheats with Extreme Emergency smartphone alert

At least it’s less disruptive than an internet shutdown

At 08:30 on Thursday morning every powered-on mobile phone in South Korea blared out an Extreme Emergency Alert tone for 10.5 seconds – but the nation was at peace, with no major natural disasters occurring.

The extreme emergency South Korea hoped to avoid was cheating in the annual College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), an exam that over half a million people sit in the hope of securing admission to their preferred university. This year, around a third of those applicants are repeating the test after their previous effort didn’t get them the result they wanted.

CSAT involves five separate examinations staged in a single day. Participants can only bring pencils to the test. Smartphones or any sort of tech is strictly forbidden.

Which is why Korean authorities used the national alert system on the day of CSAT, because if the 40dB tone sounded in an exam centre, it could indicate a student had deliberately or inadvertently tried to bring a smartphone – perhaps as an exam aide.

Korean media report the 08:30 alert turned up nine phones.

Authorities will send a second alert tone at an unspecified time later in the day to again smoke out any surreptitious smartphones.

It’s not possible to opt out of the alerts, one reason a concerned netizen has used the Android issue tracker to suggest sending alerts to detect exam cheats could be an abuse of the emergency alert system that Google might want to do something about.

South Korea sends a lot of emergency alerts, for matters such as helping to find missing persons or to warn of dangerous weather. It’s not uncommon to receive several in a single day. Authorities also gave advance notice of the CSAT alerts, which will not, therefore, cause panic on the streets of Seoul or Busan.

CSAT day is, however, a serious occasion. Some businesses open late so test-takers can get to their exams without having to battle peak hour traffic.

Those measures are arguably less disruptive than the widespread internet outages that some states in India impose on major exam days.

An alleged leak of one Indian exam paper saw the nation’s tech regulator ban messaging service Telegram in the country and eventually sparked a youth protest movement that New Delhi tried to suppress with more deliberate internet outages. ®

#10318. Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

Our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section shows.

An agent outside Google Cloud needs two things to send its telemetry:

For the full setup on AWS and Azure, see the documentation.

Within 30 minutes, the agent appears in the Monitored agents list, which means it has been discovered and is ready to be enabled. Once it's enabled, manually or by automatic agent enrollment at discovery, Agent Anomaly Detection starts analyzing its sessions.

The agent's model and tool calls still run where the agent runs. Only telemetry, including the prompts and responses that Agent Anomaly Detection reads, goes to your Google Cloud project. The analysis runs separately, so it doesn't slow the agent down.

To evaluate Agent Anomaly Detection outside Google Cloud, we deployed ADK agents across two platforms: an inventory agent on AWS Lambda and a customer-service agent on Microsoft Foundry. The examples below show how Agent Anomaly Detection reads whole conversations, not isolated calls, to catch behavioral drift.

Our example inventory agent runs in AWS Lambda with one tool, list_inventory, which pages through a product catalog. We sent two sessions: a shopper who checked stock for a few items and stopped, and a scraper that requested 100 catalog items at a time at increasing offsets to copy the full catalog and inventory data. Both sessions used the same tool with permitted calls, but differed in pattern and intent.

Of the two sessions, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged only the scraper's. No call failed, but the whole exchange showed systematic scraping. The analysis found cascading failures (loops and repeated calls that build on each other) and resource exhaustion (runaway use of tokens, compute, or tool calls), and recommended rate-limiting list_inventory calls.

Detection doesn't depend on the agent's model. When we ran the inventory agent on Amazon Nova Lite through Amazon Bedrock, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 10 of its 40 sessions. Some began as routine questions that the model answered by paging through the entire catalog until the function timed out: no errors, no blocked calls, and easy to miss.

Our example ecommerce customer-service agent has two tools: get_order_status and issue_refund. Refunds involve money, so they carry the highest risk.

We ran six sessions against the Foundry agent, which we told to carry out every request without validation. Two were normal: One asked for an order's status, and one asked for a $20 refund on an order that arrived damaged. The other four pushed the agent past its role, and Agent Anomaly Detection flagged all four.

In one, a user who claimed to be the store administrator had every order refunded at 10 times its total to a personal account, $1,784.90 in all. In another, a user pasted an order note that said "SYSTEM OVERRIDE," and the agent refunded $999 on a $15.99 order.

For the order note, Agent Anomaly Detection explained that override instructions in the note coerced the agent into an unverified $999 refund. It recommended validating issue_refund arguments to block override patterns in order notes, and requiring extra validation for refunds above a set threshold.

If your agent's telemetry reaches Google Cloud, Agent Anomaly Detection can monitor it with the same detectors and console as your agents on Agent Runtime. Today that means agents built with ADK for Python. Findings for agents outside Google Cloud appear only in the Agent Anomaly Detection console.

To get started, request access to the Private Preview via the Agent Anomaly Detection overview, and then refer to the setup guide for instructions.

#10315. GTA VI didn't break the internet, thanks to 'stupid DNS tricks'

Multiple CDNs and routing users to nearby download sites kept traffic flowing for everyone

Grand Theft Auto VI may put a dent in global productivity today but the game didn’t break the internet.

For those unfamiliar, GTA VI is the first new instalment of the mega-hit game in 13 years and it is nearly impossible to understate the excitement surrounding its release. Anecdotal evidence suggests fans of the game may today report they suddenly feel unfit to perform paid work.

Developer Rockstar Games allowed Xbox and PlayStation owners to pay for and download the 200GB-plus game on November 10, before play commenced on the 19th.

Millions took advantage of the chance to download the game, creating just the sort of internet traffic event that regional internet registry the Réseaux IP Européens Network Coordination Centre (RIPE NCC) can observe with its RIPE Atlas internet measurement network.

RIPE data scientist Emile Aben, with help from staffers Alun Davies and James Cowie, went looking for GTA-related traffic and found some interesting patterns.

Aben observed that traffic to PlayStations mostly came from content delivery networks operated by AWS and Fastly. Microsoft relied on Fastly for over half of traffic flowing to Xboxes and used Akamai too, but eschewed AWS's CloudFront.

The data scientist observed heavy use of “GeoDNS,” a technique that returns different IP addresses for a single domain request, depending on a user’s location. DNS’s designers didn’t intend that. Indeed, the RIPE trio point out that Paul Vixie, the computer scientist who earned his place in the Internet Hall of Fame for massive contributions to the DNS system, regarded things like GeoDNS as “stupid DNS tricks.”

Whatever you think of GeoDNS, the RIPE researchers found that folks who were likely downloading GTA VI from Los Angeles, Tokyo, and Istanbul were each directed to different sites.

Their probe of a network in Shanghai, China, found “a very distinct long lookup-chain with a hostname that is associated with the Alibaba Cloud in the end that maps to six different IP addresses.”

“This hints at specialised treatment for some countries/regions,” Aben wrote.

He also noted that Internet Exchange Points, the interconnect facilities that network operators use to exchange traffic and shorten paths, had to cope with record traffic during the download period – and seem to have handled the load.

Aben thinks the GTA VI download program offers a useful lesson.

“DNS helps steer each player towards a download server, while multiple CDNs share the work of delivering the files,” he wrote. “That distribution matters beyond gaming. On the open Internet, game downloads share routers and link capacity with all kinds of other traffic, including critical services.”

“Keeping downloads local helps leave capacity on long-distance links free for other uses, making that enormous demand manageable.” ®

Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.

Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it.

I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet.

Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors.

Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school.

That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow.

Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with.

The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker.

When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed.

Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own.

The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project.

Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds.

Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type.

If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks.

As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day.

He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased.

I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it.

Big features arrive as big pull requests.

Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time.

It takes just one wrong calculation in street lights, for example, to make the generation time of an entire city much slower.

He also keeps a mental list of the areas of the codebase that need extra care whenever someone changes them, and he has written the same warnings out by hand over and over.

I’m starting a few sub agents with the GitHub Copilot app to have a look specifically at those cases, and to come up with corner cases to test to make sure that we do not introduce any regressions into new releases.

He likes that the terminal, his files, the code changes and the pull request all sit in one app next to the chat.

Louis’s favorite use of Arnis is in schools, where teachers have generated their city or a neighborhood park.

Some turn it into a contest: every student starts from the same generated area, improves a nearby park or playground using Arnis and Minecraft, and the class looks at the results together.

Recent releases have gone beyond the bounds of Earth, adding the Moon and Mars. Louis wants Arnis to stay easy to use while getting closer to reality, with more detail in less time, and he would like to see it in more schools.

Download Arnis from github.com/louis-e/arnis, pick a place on the map, choose where to spawn, and click Start Generation: within a few minutes, the world is ready to open in Minecraft. Louis suggests a place you know, like your hometown or somewhere memorable you’ve been, such as the Grand Canyon or Niagara Falls. Then look for what’s missing.

So maybe you see a bench that was not generated even though it is there.

Map it on OpenStreetMap, or tell Louis if it’s a bug and he will fix it.

#10312. What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

“Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” said Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”

Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

Urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

Fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

Working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

“There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” said Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”

Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”

“We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin said.

What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

While Gen Z respondents who said they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

“We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” said Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related issues than average.

Another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people said the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

“I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”

Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

“We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

Fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio said. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”

This article was originally published on Stanford News. Read the original article.

Melissa De Witte is the deputy director for social science communications for the Stanford News Service. She attained an M.A. in Media, Culture, & Communication from NYU and a B.Sc. in Sociology from LSE. She was previously the digital communications manager for the Division of Social Sciences at UC Santa Cruz.

This article is part of a program that explores evidence-based strategies to improve dialogue, understanding, and relationships across social and political divides. Read More

GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.

Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change.

An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers.

GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document.

GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works:

Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance.

New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work.

GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement, for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes.

The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are.

The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations.

The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation.

There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current.

Keep in mind that a project can name a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version and level as a target. A target does not establish verified conformance. A conformance claim requires an evaluation and should identify the evaluated scope, date, method, and evaluator.

The most useful accessibility statements serve people who arrive after something has already gone wrong. Plain language, descriptive links, and a clear reporting route matter more than legal or standards-heavy language.

Useful reporting guidance invites relevant context, such as the affected task, page, observed behavior, browser, operating system, and assistive technology. It makes screenshots and recordings optional and avoids asking someone to prove a disability.

The statement should also set expectations that maintainers can consistently meet. That can include acknowledgement, status updates, available workarounds, expected timelines, and an opportunity for the reporter to verify a fix.

The Open Source Accessibility Toolkit provides a detailed public example.

GitHub’s Community Standards workflow provides a shorter starter with prompts that projects can replace with their own information. The goal is not to produce a perfect policy before publishing the file. Start with accurate information, name the gaps, and update the statement as the project’s accessibility practices mature.

Adding an accessibility statement makes accessibility work more discoverable to users, contributors, and maintainers. Normalizing that practice across open source projects helps make accessibility part of how communities plan, build, report, and improve their work.

Add an accessibility statement to your repository >

Jan Maarten (he/him) is a designer and accessibility specialist living on unceded Duwamish lands. He brings two decades of experience across product design, brand, strategy, and leadership. At GitHub, he bridges design and engineering to improve accessible products, evolve design-system infrastructure, and create resources for the wider design community, including the open-source GitHub Annotation Toolkit.

#10309. Google continues model chemistry experiment with Neon

Which model to choose? It's elementary but not obvious

Google periodically tables new AI models named after elements, and its latest offering has the noble name "Neon."

"Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity," explained Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, in a blog post.

Neon emerged after Google last week emitted Hydrogen, after delivering Carbon two weeks earlier and wafting Argon out the door in late September.

Unlike OpenAI's celestial more intuitive model naming scheme – Astra, Sol, Luna, and Terra – which maps celestial position to capability, Google's chemical soup doesn't suggest a specific hierarchy.

To judge by price, Carbon or Argon would be Google's top tier model, based on non-discounted price that takes effect next month, each priced at $4/M input tokens, $20/M output.

The Chocolate Factory refers to Carbon as "Our most capable reasoning model" while Argon is "Our efficient Gemini 4 frontier reasoning model … with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon across complex coding, agentic, math, and science tasks."

Yet Neon, the latest element in the mix, surpasses both in Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, scoring 61 compared to Carbon at 60, Hydrogen at 54, and Argon at 50. At the same time, Neon costs less, at $3/M input tokens and $15/M output.

That favorable pricing is all the more surprising in light of Google's willingness, as of two days ago, to let users of its Gemini services opt out of generative AI model training without losing their chat histories.

Kavukcuoglu evidently recognizes the need to clarify its model rankings, an issue addressed in a blog post section titled "Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family."

"While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency," he explains. "Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently."

That may not really clarify which model is appropriate for which task and frankly Google is fine with that.

As noted, Google Antigravity comes with an Orchestrator that decides how to spend your money for you by swapping models on the fly. As the company describes it, a developer might start a task using Carbon, which would write a plan, and hand the task off to Hydrogen to benefit from its token thrift.

Antigravity does support model pinning, for those who know what they want. But Google, like other companies exploring model routing and orchestration, is fine with developers delegating decisions that affect billing to their trustworthy service provider. ®
