#10258. You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

It’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a new paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”

These people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

If you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

In our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”

They highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”

Rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

In many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

However, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person said.

Some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another said, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”

Rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

One person said, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”

It’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person said.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series

Meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly important for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”

Naming rustout won’t solve the issue, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

From my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

One participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others said, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”

In such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

The language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

They may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once said, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

If you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

For organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

That is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

Sabrina Fitzsimons, Ph.D., is a lecturer at Dublin City University, Ireland. Her research combines expertise in educators’ occupational well-being, mental health, and online environments.

Introducing Replica and the Open Source Accessibility Framework, new open source projects for collaboration and inclusion.

In 2026, public contributions on GitHub soared to 2.5 billion, more than double last year’s total of 1.12 billion. It goes to show how open source remains a powerful mechanism for developers to build, share, and grow communities.

Open source is how I began my GitHub journey. I contributed to Processing Foundation by adding alt-text to images on the p5.js website. This was the first time I felt included in a software development space as someone with a background in traditional fine arts and design. It was the first time I made a fork, opened a pull request, and merged code on a repo that wasn’t mine.

Working at GitHub, you hear stories like mine everywhere. Open source is foundational to us not only as a business but also for who we are as the people who build it! We recently launched two new open source projects to share with the community: Replica, an open-source design harness, and the Open Source Accessibility Framework.

I attended John Maeda’s session with Qianqian Ye, Director of Creative Technology at Processing Foundation, at GitHub Universe titled, “Sketching with code in the age of AI.” This session talked about the power of the open source community and reminded me how important it is to our developer ecosystem. Open source accelerates innovation. It is the reason AI tooling understands different coding languages so well, how developers hacked agent harnesses to be more efficient, and why new AI companies have formed.

This moment resonated with me. Qianqian asked:

“What do you think the role open-source community plays nowadays in the age of AI?”

“I worked in the WordPress open source community, where I learned that PHP stands for people helping people. And so if anything, I’m just sort of optimistic that the open source world is the way of how we should do things in general, in society. And I’m really excited how, at GitHub, we care so deeply about open source.”

In 2025, 60% of the top growing open source projects were AI focused. At GitHub, it is no different. A few weeks ago, GitHub’s design team introduced Replica, which considers the role of designers in the era of AI and focuses on reinforcement learning. Replica started as an internal project, but it proved to be so useful that our design team shared the tool so developers and designers everywhere could also benefit.

GitHub Replica does a lot of reinforcement learning. It’s an open source design harness to enable you to do the kind of things you hope to do in prototyping playground

With Replica, anyone can create AI-generated prototypes within their design system and refine them side-by-side with GitHub Copilot. You can also publish prototypes to a Replica Hub to collaborate with teammates, receive comments, and iterate.

With reinforcement learning top of mind, the system learns what good looks like from each interaction and from the comments on the prototypes; it gets better over time. Because Replica is open source, you can hack it and adapt it to fit your teams’ products and workflows however you see fit.

Developers pushed code changes to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the last year, more than 2024 and 2025 combined. Commits across all repo types (public and private) climbed even faster to 34.3 billion, more than three times where they stood two years ago. Merged pull requests more than tripled to 1.3 billion over the same period, an average of 3.5 million a day. AI has helped us all build faster. With this volume, and more to be expected, we must keep accessibility top of mind so that the code that is being shipped is accessible to all.

As the home for all developers, we want every developer to feel welcome and to be able to contribute to the future of global software development using everything GitHub has to offer.

The Open Source Accessibility Framework, created in collaboration with external contributors from the disability and accessibility communities, launched last month. It helps make accessibility an inherent part of how projects are created. It is an accountability model with four phases so developers can turn projects and accessibility goals into public, trackable progress. A core component of this is the new ACCESSIBILITY.md file, a file now visible on repository overview pages, giving a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers. Read more about the ACCESSIBILITY.md file.

Going back to John and Qianqian’s Universe talk, John asked:

“How does an open source community keep something lasting that long? What’s the secret?”

“I think the secret is one of the most obvious ones. Community.”

The GitHub repo firstcontributions/first-contributions ranked fourth among the fastest-growing community projects in 2026 by contributors, helping developers take their first steps into open source. We hope you can join our open-source community: hack away at our new projects or start your own.

Watch John Maeda and Qianqian Ye’s session 👇

#10255. Europe's biggest gas supplier battling cyberattack – with no timeline for recovery

Norwegian energy giant Equinor says oil and gas production remains unaffected

Norwegian energy giant Equinor is battling a cyberattack on its IT systems, though the company insists that hackers haven't disrupted its oil and gas production.

Equinor, Europe's largest supplier of natural gas, first disclosed the attack on Tuesday evening, saying it had called in the relevant resources to deal with the intrusion and had found no indication that any data had been stolen.

In an update on Wednesday, the company said it had a better handle on how the attack was carried out and which of its systems had been compromised, though it stopped short of sharing either of those details.

"As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading," Equinor said. The company added that it had found nothing to suggest the incident would affect employees, partners, or suppliers.

In a further update on Thursday, Equinor said the attack remained ongoing but did not appear to be specifically targeting the company. Production continued normally, with no indications that data had been stolen or altered. The incident has been reported to police.

What kind of attack Equinor is dealing with remains a mystery. The company hasn't identified those responsible, disclosed whether it's received any demands from the hackers, or said when it expects the affected systems to be fully restored.

The Register has asked Equinor to elaborate, including whether any of its UK operations have been affected and whether the hackers managed to venture beyond its corporate IT network.

Equinor spokesperson Ellen Maria Skjelsbæk told Norwegian news agency NTB that the company hadn't lost access to its IT systems, though staff could have trouble accessing some corporate applications and services. Email appears to be among the casualties, with Reuters reporting that the company's internal email system was down.

Equinor, which traded as Statoil until 2018, is still largely in the hands of the Norwegian state, which owns 67 percent of the company. The oil and gas biz employs around 25,000 people and operates in more than 20 countries.

The bulk of Equinor's oil and gas production takes place off the coast of Norway, but the company also pumps oil and gas in the UK, US, Brazil, and Canada. It's one of the companies behind Dogger Bank, the enormous offshore wind project off England's northeast coast, and is also in the business of capturing and storing carbon dioxide.

Equinor's assurances about production will be particularly welcome in Europe, which has become increasingly reliant on Norwegian gas since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The attack comes just weeks after Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) raised its cyberattack risk assessment to four on a five-point scale. The agency said the number of successful cyber operations against Norwegian businesses had tripled over the preceding six months and warned of potential disruption to essential services, including water and electricity supplies.

Europe has already had a few nasty reminders this year of what happens when hackers get their hands on industrial equipment. Last week, the French government pinned a series of cyberattacks targeting refrigeration systems at more than 700 retail sites in October on a hacking unit affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The crooks turned up the temperature in supermarket fridges and freezers, ruining tens of millions of euros' worth of food and starting fires at some premises.

Nothing suggests Equinor's hackers have similar ambitions, or that they've got anywhere near the kit used to extract and transport oil and gas. Given how much of Europe depends on that kit continuing to work, a little more detail from the Norwegian energy giant wouldn't go amiss. ®

#10253. Russian national accused of stalking San Francisco techie in plot against US defense-tech giant

DoJ claims suspect part of 4-month operation to steal secrets, surveil employees

A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech company in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes.

Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent.

After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company.

Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war.

While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation.

D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July.

The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the company’s employees.

In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device.

The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims.

D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so.

One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong.

D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots.

The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler.

Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but  claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date.

The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations.

According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 showed that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US.

Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram.

A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp.

The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico.

Records obtained from Google showed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the company's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints.

The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto company’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers.

Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing.

D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash.

The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco.

The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed company's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed.

Contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else.

The affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept.

These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a New York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns."

He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing.

One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there.

FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being:

A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for company employees’ homes

Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses.

Per the affidavit, D'iu was said to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex.

"D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated.

At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the company he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government.

Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources.

"D'iu's targeting of the company and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine."

The Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®

#10252. Can Community Programs Reduce Gun Violence?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

A new study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years.

According to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera.

Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, said, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.”

Homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence.

According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who currently serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.”

According to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study shows Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally.

According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook.

One former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.”

The paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma.

This article was originally published on Berkeley Public Health News. Read the original article.

UC Berkeley School of Public Health has been a global health leader in research innovation, educational excellence, and social impact for more than 75 years.

His face will melt and his arse will freeze. This is of course ignoring thermal transfer through the astronauts body itself.

It also points to the problem with all this space datacenter malarky. A datacenter floatimg in space has two very contradictory needs. It needs to absob lots of energy to power it. It needs to expel lots of energy to avoid it melting into slag. Unfortunately if its in the sun, it means it will struggle radiating heat because the temperatures from direct energy transfering into it is so much higher than what it wants to radiate. Try cooling something on a boiling hot day. yeah. On the other hand it wants to radiate its heat away. It cant convect, it cant conduct heat. It can only radiate heat, and its best placed to do that shielded from the sun.

In other words it needs its solar panels in the sun where its super hot and its radiator panels in darkness where its super cold. ANd while you could I suppose do some clever engineering and stick solar input on one side of the panel and the radiator on the other, those two things are physically connected and conduction will completely neutralize any radiator dead in its tracks.

I cant see a solution that isn't massively huge and orders of magnitude more expensive than the blindingly obvious solution to all of these problems;- Just put the fucking things in the ocean. wave and wind power to run the datacenter, and a giant monster sized ocean made of water to cool it.

True, but we're talking about Earth orbit, which isn't anywhere near a perfect vacuum. At 500 km the atmosphere is around a thousand Kelvin and any solar wind particles you run into are in the tens of thousands up to a million or so.

What you have for instance are photons from the Cosmic Background radiation, whose temperature is 2.7 K. But you also have cosmic rays, whose temperature can go into billions of degrees (Fahrenheit, Kelvin, Celsius, does not matter in this case). And because they don't interact with each other, they don't give you an average temperature.

That means that Space is essentially without any temperature, but that means in turn that you can't lose heat by heat exchange, because for that, you would need particle interaction. All that's left is Black Body radiation, and at temperatures around 300 K, you get a radiation of around 450 Watts per square meter of surface. And be aware that none of the surfaces should face each other and especially, all have to face away from the Sun.

#10246. NAND prices tipped to fall as Chinese cloud giants cut SSD orders

TrendForce sees supply outpacing demand in 2027, though cheaper flash won't fix the DRAM squeeze

NAND flash prices could start falling next year as Chinese cloud operators cut enterprise SSD orders, helping push the market toward oversupply.

Taiwan-based market intelligence firm TrendForce says Chinese cloud service providers are grappling with GPU shortages, high inventories, and fierce competition over AI token pricing.

As a result, they have reduced their total enterprise SSD orders for 2027 by a substantial amount. Although TrendForce doesn't specify any figures, it says the cutbacks in China are large enough to outweigh the additional demand coming from US-based cloud operators.

But don't get too excited: TrendForce forecasts overall NAND flash contract prices falling by 0-5 percent quarter on quarter in early 2027, with all product categories entering a downturn from the second quarter.

Falling orders are only half the story. Manufacturers are also increasing output, while weaker consumer electronics sales could further depress demand.

Strong demand for high-performance storage in the US continues to drive manufacturers to expand capacity and upgrade to newer process technologies. At the same time, the rising adoption of quad-level cell (QLC) technology and increasing number of layers in the NAND chips will further boost bit output, TrendForce observes.

Some suppliers may go slower on their expansion plans in response to sluggish consumer demand, but the firm still expects global NAND flash output, measured in storage capacity, to grow by 25 to 30 percent in 2027.

US restrictions on access to advanced AI chips could put Chinese cloud operators under further pressure. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has introduced new restrictions on sales of GPUs, and on remote access to them via the cloud.

The new restrictions "set everyone back in China," as The Register reported.

TrendForce adds the caveat to its forecast that its market outlook depends on factors such as the pace of inventory reduction among Chinese CSPs, further changes to the restrictions on overseas GPU procurement, and whether device makers continue reducing storage capacities in 2028.

Sadly, cheaper NAND wouldn't resolve the separate squeeze on DRAM supplies. The situation, caused by memory makers opting to produce high-margin products for the AI market rather than mainstream chips, has already increased prices of PCs in Europe by double-digit percentages, leading to a fall in shipments as buyers balk at the cost. ®

#10243. How Love Saves Lives

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

When someone takes his own life, the grief of parents, lovers, children, and friends can be unspeakable. At a memorial for one young suicide I attended a few years ago, the father of the deceased could barely walk to the altar to light a candle. Everyone was crying.

How could this talented, beautiful young person not know she’d be terribly, horribly missed?

Most experts attribute suicide to severe mental illness caused by a brain injury or genetic predisposition, or due to some other, as yet unknown, physical or chemical trigger. Severe depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia are all inordinately common among people who die by suicide.

Severe mental illnesses are no doubt responsible for many, if not most, of the eight hundred thousand or so suicides that occur around the world each year, including, perhaps, that young person’s whose memorial I attended.

My book, Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic, isn’t primarily about such cases—or about how to prevent suicide. Such a book would have detailed sections about psychotherapy, restrictions on firearms, safety barriers for bridges, and other measures that really do save lives. Instead, my aim was to explore why some people want to take their own lives in the first place and how that desire might be reduced, in both individuals and communities.

Having spent the past few years reading about suicide, speaking with scores of people who’ve experienced suicidal feelings, and having experienced them myself from time to time, I’ve come to understand that what suicidal people feel is the indifference, not of the universe, but of those closest to them. They sense that their own feelings don’t matter to the people they care most about.

These experiences are backed up by studies showing that the main reason suicidal people want to die is because they think no one cares about them. Some suicides even seem to believe they’re doing everyone a favor by taking their own lives.

Psychologist Thomas Joiner, who’s been studying suicide for thirty years, calls it a force of nature that distorts people’s minds so they become convinced that they are a burden to others and no one wants them around. In study after study, the most common trigger for suicide is a perceived rupture in a close relationship, either with a lover, parent, or other close relative, that seems irreparable to the suicidal person.

Given that suicide seems driven by fraught or broken connections, it’s perhaps not surprising that I also discovered that suicide can spread within social groups like a disease. The suicide rate of particular groups can jump—sometimes increasing three- or four-fold or more—in a short time, meaning it behaves like an epidemic, like malaria during the rainy season or flu in the fall. Suicide epidemics unfold more slowly than these microbial plagues—over years or decades, not weeks or months—but they happen far too quickly to result from genetic changes, and affect far too many people to be explained away as spontaneous cases of biologically caused mental illness or brain injury. The causes therefore must have something to do with the changing social environment in which these people live. Suicide epidemics have occurred on virtually every continent.

What’s scary about this is that it means suicide could come for any of us. The very existence of suicide epidemics proves that people with suicidal feelings aren’t a species apart. Anyone can feel suicidal under certain conditions—and the key to stopping suicide epidemics is to change those conditions.

I teach and write about public health and have long been fascinated by epidemics because they always tell a story. In most literary depictions of epidemics, such as Albert Camus’s The Plague or Daniel Defoe’s A Journal of the Plague Year, they seem to strike from nowhere, but this isn’t how epidemics typically behave. Individual cases of disease are hard to predict. Some of us will become ill tomorrow, but there’s no telling who. Even those who take risks may well escape the consequences.

First, it’s important to understand what doesn’t. Suicide isn’t more common during wars or where people are poorer or have recently experienced some environmental disaster like a flood, earthquake, or wildfire. Suicide was common among African slaves, especially on the ships en route to America and when they first arrived, but despite segregation, police brutality, mass incarceration, and other outrages, the suicide rate of African Americans has been generally lower than that of U.S. whites since record-keeping began in the 1930s.

What seems to matter is whether people believe someone, somewhere, really cares about and understands them.

The mental pain that drives suicide is really the flip side of love, says Israeli neuroscientist Yoram Yovell. “It probably evolved along with motherhood. . . . Inherent in us are very strong emotional forces that function to keep mothers and babies together. When they get too far from each other, they feel mental pain,” which we experience when we search for love. This is why “so many children’s stories are about a boy looking for his lost mother.”

Evidence supports Yovell’s theory. A 1999 study found that some 78% of high lethality suicide attempters had recently experienced the loss of a close personal relationship, and suicide notes often express love for those left behind. In 2012, Zimri Yaseen and his colleagues reported that suicidal people interviewed in emergency rooms were especially likely to report that in the three preceding days, they’d felt “unusually intense or deep feelings of love,” which they presumably also felt were not reciprocated.

But why would large groups of people—from the islands of Micronesia to the Arctic Circle, from the cities of post-communist Russia to the towns of contemporary America—suddenly begin questioning their most intimate attachments? How does love suddenly disappear—or seem to—from the lives of thousands of people?

In my book, Why Live, I argue that it has to do with how we internalize socioeconomic change.

The first well-researched suicide epidemic occurred across Western Europe during the 19th century. Intellectuals debated the causes as we debate the vicissitudes of the stock market. Rising suicide rates were attributed to socialism, atmospheric moisture, the vice of masturbation, and the Romantic era inclination to preserve—through death—the passions of youth against the onslaught of Bourgeois boredom brought on by industrialization and urban life.

Doctors even searched, in vain, for a “suicidogenic” organ in the cadavers of people who’d died by suicide. But others blamed society, that collective property of human groups that shapes our thinking and behavior.

As a Jew growing up in France amid increasing anti-Semitism, Émile Durkheim had seen how shared values and beliefs buffered his people against the effects of discrimination and how anti-Semitism tightened bonds among them. He went on to become one of the founders of sociology, which is the study of those bonds: what holds us together, what drives us apart, and what happens as a result.

In his 1897 book, Suicide, Durkheim theorized that suicides increase wherever society is fragmenting and people are growing more detached from one another: where divorce rates are higher, for example, and where Protestants, with their individualistic culture and aloofness from collective ritual, outnumber Catholics. He likened it to entropy—the universal tendency toward chaos and disorder at the atomic level discovered by physicists earlier in the century. Appearing on the eve of humanity’s, as yet, bloodiest century, Durkheim’s book seemed to foreshadow the trouble to come.

What is it about fragmenting societies that causes mental pain?

Durkheim was vague, even a little loopy, when it came to explaining this. At the time, psychologists were just discovering the unconscious, which they explored through studies of hypnosis and hallucinations. Durkheim followed this research closely, and believed that values and meanings flowed through populations like electrical currents, as if societies had what scholars Laurent Mucchielli and Marc Renneville refer to as a “collective soul.” These currents could change people’s behavior through unconscious mechanisms, just as changes in temperature and pressure change the behavior of molecules.

Many late-19th-century scientists believed that our brains generated signals analogous to radio waves. Alexander Graham Bell, Nikola Tesla, and James Clerk Maxwell even wired up helmets and other gizmos to try to measure them. Mark Twain told Harper’s Monthly that thoughts could shoot from brain to brain, without their owners having to open their mouths to communicate. Likewise, Durkheim maintained that whatever suicidal people said about their feelings were just expressions of resolutions planted in their minds by the vibes of a disintegrating society.

The brain-wave theory eventually fell out of fashion. In the 1930s, one of Durkheim’s protégés came closer to explaining the psychological effects of social fragmentation. Maurice Halbwachs taught at the University of Strasbourg from 1919 until his death in a Nazi concentration camp in 1945. His 1930 monograph The Causes of Suicide identified an existential loneliness that, if not entirely new, flourished in the growing towns and cities of 19th-century Europe and the countryside they engulfed.

According to Halbwachs, cities create opportunities for social and economic advancement, but they also create the conditions for exploitative relationships, swindles, romantic betrayals, fragile friendships, broken families, unstable jobs, and many other sources of despair.

As European cities grew, so did a new class of people who were particularly prone to suicide, including abandoned lovers, lonely widowers, workers who’d lost their jobs, nobles shamed by some dishonorable act, gamblers who couldn’t pay their debts, merchants who’d ruined themselves, heirs who’d squandered their fortunes, and others who’d suffered a common bitter fate: sudden exclusion from a cherished social community. As Halwachs writes:

They all see their social level lowered. They are to a certain extent declassed. But what does it mean to be declassed? It is to pass from a group that one knows, that esteems you, to another that ignores you and whose appreciation one has no reason to hold. One then feels a void opening around oneself. Those who once surrounded you, with whom you had so many ideas in common, so many prejudices in common, with whom so many affinities brought you together because you found yourself in them as they found yourself in you, suddenly move away. You disappear from their concerns and their memory. Those among whom you find yourself understand neither your disorientation, nor your nostalgia and your regrets. Detached from the group by a sudden shock, you are incapable, or at least you believe yourself incapable, of ever finding in another any support, nor anything to replace what you have lost.

In the midst of the 19th-century suicide crisis, the very meaning of the word “lonely” changed, from an adjective typically used to describe empty places and people who stood alone before God to one with the emotional and psychological connotations it has for us today. Suicidal despair, Halbwachs wrote, had been rarer in the past because traditional rural life was simpler and more predictable:

We lived on the spot . . . adapted to each other, knowing each other too well to be frequently exposed to the clashes that occur when we move from one place, one situation, one profession, to another. Business carried less risk. Ambitions were less aroused, humiliations rarer. We thought and felt in common. Sorrows and troubles, instead of concentrating within the consciousness of this or that individual, dispersed and died out within the group.

What Halbwachs was describing was the transition from what German sociologist Ferdinand Tönnies called Gemeinschaft, or communities based on trust, mutual respect, and sharing of whatever material goods one had, to Gesellschaft, societies based largely on market transactions and political calculation in which ties of friendship and loyalty are relegated to private family life, and may not even reliably be found there.

As far as I’ve been able to determine, wherever that transition has occurred, a suicide epidemic has followed swiftly behind.

But there is another ingredient, too. As villagers shifted away from subsistence and small-scale farming to wage labor and trade, their intimate relationships became both more fragile and more precious. The extended family, which once formed a social mesh that supported everyone, waned in significance, and walls rose up around increasingly private and nuclearized families, usually dominated by a single, generally male breadwinner, upon whom everyone else in the family depended. If you felt your family didn’t respect and care about you, you were in a new sort of trouble, not just because the community no longer offered you a livelihood, but because your whole identity was at stake.

Modern capitalist society creates, in all of us, something of the double consciousness described by the great African American sociologist W. E. B. DuBois. When a modern person looks at a stranger, he wonders not only, as his villager ancestors did, “What can I do to help this person? And is he the kind of person who will help me?” but “What does that stranger see when he looks at me? What essence does he detect? A beauty or a beast? A success or a failure? A respectable person or a fool?”

The answer sometimes comes as a disappointment. In traditionally cohesive societies, this mattered less, because a person’s worth was measured by what he did for others, and everyone was capable of contributing something. You might not be the best hunter, fisherman, storyteller, or drummer; you might not be the best grower of breadfruit or builder of igloos; but you still mattered. Only the greedy and selfish were looked down upon and excluded.

In modern societies, generosity still counts, but for far less than it used to. If others find us wanting—because of our looks, talents, graces, bank accounts, intelligence, or for whatever reason—we are alone with it, and must make sense of it, somehow.

For most of us, what makes modern life, with all its loneliness and insecurity, bearable are close relationships with people we count on to see and accept us for who we really are—whatever our flaws. Romantic rejection is exquisitely painful because we feel that that special quality within us, the thing that makes us lovable—and everyone has something—has either been unrecognized or, worse, seen and rejected.

The pain of rejection by a parent or other close relative is even worse because it can make us feel as though no one could ever understand and sympathize with us. After all, they know us best of all.

In the absence of an abstract sense of group belonging, interpersonal love, especially between parents and children and romantic partners, has become the main source of our psychological resilience, our ability to withstand the disappointments encountered in the outside world, just as the mutually reinforcing group gave strength to our ancestors fighting for survival on the plains, tundras, beaches, and forests of the past.

Love is not just a feeling; it’s also a culture, which developed fairly recently, first in Western societies, and then around the world on the heels of capitalism, modernity, and individualism. It’s no coincidence, the social philosopher Erich Fromm pointed out, that as modern ways of life displaced the traditional, cohesive village and clan, love poems, songs, and stories came to occupy the center of Western culture, displacing archaic tales of heroism and godliness.

It’s not that love was absent from the art of the ancient past, but as often as not, it was seen as a cause of calamity and human folly. Think of Helen of Troy, Dido and Aeneas, Adam and Eve. Then, more or less in lockstep with commercial culture and urbanization, love came to be seen as a force superior to the gods or God or honor or historic destiny.

The behavior of parents and spouses changed, too. Until the 1800s, childrearing in England, for example, was seen as an exercise less in nurturing than in training for adulthood. Men who were fed up with their wives could sell them at markets or abandon them and marry someone else without divorcing. Infants who died weren’t even listed in parish registers. Only in the 19th century did heartfelt observations of sons and daughters begin appearing regularly in the diaries of American and English mothers.

With the growth of markets and formal state institutions, people came to rely less on kinship networks for social welfare and trade and the family gradually shifted from an economic enterprise to a child-centered haven in a heartless world. The 1700s saw the first toy shops, women’s magazines, popular child care manuals, and family portraits. Christian churches, which had previously stressed family discipline and sometimes even the virtues of wife-beating, now promoted ideals of conjugal and parental love.

Today, birthday parties, children’s allowances, and Valentine’s Day cards are symbols we use to assure each other that our most important relationships are real. Meanwhile, parenting manuals, happily-ever-after fairy tales, Hollywood movies, and the novels of Jane Austen, George Eliot, Charles Dickens, Barbara Cartland, Colleen Hoover, and countless others illustrate the enactment of love according to Western norms.

Premodern Europeans, as well as Indigenous groups the world over, didn’t need this culture because in the mutual aid communities of bygone days, you knew who you were and what you needed to do to gain the esteem of others: You had to pitch in for the group. You helped others and they helped you. That was love, and according to accounts of anthropologists, it was everywhere, as ubiquitous as air.

But when these groups modernized, in some cases very rapidly under the forces of capitalism and colonialism, the rules changed. Now it was unclear what the common goals were and what others were looking for in us. If they didn’t like us, there wasn’t a lot we could do about it. If the people we loved—our romantic partners, parents, and children—felt that way, it was intolerably painful because our hearts had nowhere to turn. Every rejection could now elicit devastating feelings of aloneness. “Who am I?” we are left to wonder. “Am I worth anything at all to anyone?”

Signifiers of love—birthday cards and so on—aren’t enough. We need the confidence that our own feelings are understood. Some people, either because of the distortions of mental illness or because they really are lost and alone, simply don’t have it.

But all is not lost. As I argue in Why Live, communities can regrow, just like decimated forests. The best policy I can think of is to strive for greater economic equality, which will naturally reduce insecurity, and, in turn, foster greater spiritual as well as material generosity. We are kinder to one another when we don’t feel threatened. Otherwise, the best advice I can think of is not to make things worse. When positive communities begin to emerge, the trick is not to ruin them.

Let’s treat communities like ecosystems so that every time a major economic policy shift is proposed—a massive new trade deal or development project—the effects on communities are considered, and the preservation of Gemeinschaft is prioritized. Ideally, studies of this, analogous to the environmental impact studies now required by all World Bank loans to developing countries, would be conducted with the full and meaningful involvement of affected communities.

Some elements of Gemeinschaft survive, even in these harsh times—in well-functioning neighborhoods, in friendship networks, sometimes in the military, and in some schools and workplaces. You know it when you see it; it’s where you feel your dignity is recognized. In defending and building that, we give everyone more reason to live.

Helen C. Epstein, Ph.D., is visiting professor of global public health and human rights at Bard College. She is the author of Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic and Another Fine Mess: America, Uganda, and the War on Terror.

By focusing on culture, family, and community, Jasmin Brooks Stephens says we can support mental health in Black youth long before crises occur.

A therapist explains how having kids can change our perspective on how our parents treated us, for better or worse.

Couples who embrace their own “microculture”—pet names, inside jokes, and rituals—may be happier and more satisfied with their relationship.

Do you embrace a diversity of backgrounds and opinions in others?

What does it actually take to put people over politics? Republican and Democrat students discover ways to resist the pull to demean or villainize people with whom they strongly disagree.

What if you could fall in love, or forge deep connections, in just 45 minutes? Our guests, Kristen Meinzer and Jolenta Greenberg of By The Book podcast, try out 36 questions with their partners to see if they can strengthen their connection.

The Greater Good Science Center studies the psychology, sociology, and neuroscience of well-being, and teaches skills that foster a thriving, resilient, and compassionate society.

#10241. Anthropic throws open doors at $2T valuation as shares pop 34% in initial trading

Company still has to contend with massive compute obligations and the threat of open models, neither of which Dario Amodei is worried about, he claims

Welcome to the world of public AI frontier labs: Anthropic is now a publicly-held company with its Thursday IPO, and investors are clamoring for a piece of the pie, for now anyway.

That $83 IPO price didn’t last long, with shares rocketing to $111.50 by the time the public could get their hands on them at the end of the initial auction. That means that the company was valued at around $2 trillion as of the public availability of the 980 million shares it put up for sale, a 34 percent increase over the IPO price.

At just under six years old, Anthropic’s meteoric rise to that valuation has sent investors into a frenzy despite uncertainties surrounding the company’s future profitability. As we’ve noted, Anthropic is on the hook for nearly $1 trillion in compute obligations that could drag its profitability prospects down if any one of a number of scenarios happens to materialize.

Amodei was on hand to address some of those questions with CNBC this morning following the opening of markets on his company’s big day.

When asked about the risk Anthropic’s massive compute bills to its bottom line, Amodei admitted the company’s needs are difficult to predict, and that - get this - they try to err on the low side.

That’s right: The $900 billion in infrastructure and compute commitments that Anthropic revealed in a recent regulatory filing, which could end up surpassing $1T in short order, might just be an underestimate of what the company will need in coming months and years.

Not to worry, though, the Anthropic CEO insisted: It’s worth it.

“We’re willing to put into place these very large compute spends because, historically, we’ve seen that it pays off,” Amodei told CNBC’s Ross Sorkin, adding that the returns on the cognitive capabilities of its new models are “so high” as to make all that spending worth it - eventually, one would assume based on his comments, Anthropic is sure to come out on top.

But what of the threat of open models that could undermine the constant push at Anthropic and other frontier labs to create the most power-hungry, resource-intensive, and powerful AI? Bah, that’s not a problem either.

Frontier model makers like Anthropic, Amodei said, have already proven that they can do the heavy lifting at the bleeding edge, so you can trust it to make reliable models that are cheaper and less capable, too.

“Anthropic can compete both at and away from the frontier,” The Anthropic CEO said.

Whether that’ll mean long-term success for investors is another thing altogether. Mozilla president Mark Surman doesn’t think valuation translates into long-term success, for one. He told The Register this morning that the one thing he consistently hears from developers is that they want AI they can control, not rent from a frontier lab. As Amodei suggested in his comments, Anthropic is aware that those with less intense AI needs might not choose its models, and that could harm the company.

“Pushing AI toward open source matters so much right now,” Surman said in an email. “Mozilla’s own research this year found that open source models account for a third of all tokens, while the gap with the best closed models is down to about 3.3 per cent.”

In other words, keep an eye on that Anthropic stock - it might be hot now, but reality could still catch up to the company with the biggest-ever IPO.

“The market is already moving,” Surman said. “No valuation changes that.” ®

#10236. XXRI-OS explores the lowest end of the Linux desktop

Less is more, but this distro explores exactly how much less

New Linux distros seem to appear daily, but far too few distinguish themselves by being smaller and simpler.

XXRI OS is a fairly new desktop Linux distro. It has a snazzy-looking website, complete with an amusing URL, and along similar lines, its GitHub page has a very heavily formatted README. Nonetheless, this is not another over-complex opinionated slopfest of an OS with built-in AI, bizarre keystrokes, and several proprietary components. It's almost the reverse.

The main download is just 287.4 MB, and that's the full distro, not a minimalist installer that fetches most of the OS over your internet connection. We installed it in a VirtualBox VM. It took 675 MB of disk space, and in the graphical desktop, when we opened a terminal window, it reported just 75 MB of RAM in use with the desktop and terminal running. We are restraining ourselves hard when we say that those are unusually low numbers for the 2020s. We would expect most cut-down lightweight Linux distros to use around five to 10 times as much disk space or memory.

The current release of XXRI-OS is version 2.7. XXRI OS 1.0 came out in May 2025, making this a young project with five published releases already behind it. It also has much deeper roots: it is based on the existing and much older Tiny Core Linux. The Reg FOSS desk last looked at Tiny Core Linux 15 back in March 2024 and the project is still going strong: the latest version is version 17.1.

Tiny Core Linux is a marvel, but there are prices to pay for somehow getting a graphical Linux desktop into a 23 MB download. It runs from RAM and uses its own extension-based package system, which can make adding components and managing updates unfamiliar territory. XXRI OS takes TCL and turns it into a slightly more conventional desktop.

It installs to disk in the usual way, and it includes the core functions that most people would expect from their OS in 2026. It has a file manager, a text editor, a media player, a simple app store for adding further components, and a settings app including an update manager. It even includes its own web browser, and there are both x86-32 and x86-64 variants.

The desktop layout has a floating dock at bottom center, and the icons are unlabelled. To save you some guesswork, though, floating just to the left of the dock is an icon with a grid of dots, which is an app launcher. The icons in that do have text labels underneath, so you can learn which symbol denotes which function from here.

We plan to experiment more with this remarkable little OS and see how well it runs on the oldest, slowest boxes in the Irish Sea wing of Vulture Towers, but we like what we see so far. It's an impressive experiment in how low Linux can go and remain useful. While Tiny Core Linux goes down to Windows 95 levels of resource usage, XXRI OS has a more usable Windows 2000-level baseline. Over a quarter of a century later, that is nearly unbeatable. ®

#10235. In the Face of Crisis, Psychologists Urge a Return to the Basics

As numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by new technology, global crises, and loneliness. What do the nation’s psychologists recommend? At the annual convention of the American Psychological Association last month in Washington D.C., that turned out to be a return to the basics: tending to our bodies, connecting in-person, and caring for each other and the most marginalized among us. Joy D. Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing. The chronic stress builds up over time and becomes biological harm, Calloway said, citing the weathering theory described by Arline Geronimus, a public health researcher at the University of Michigan. Calloway continued: The field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness. . . . Perhaps our greatest blind spot is that we’ve confused resilience with wellness. . . . While wellness begins with individuals, it is nurtured by families, strengthened by communities, and made possible by the systems, institutions, and policies that create the conditions for people to thrive. We don’t simply practice wellness; we build it collectively. Over three days, nearly 8,000 people from 60 different countries attended the conference in person, participating in a program that included 523 different sessions and 1,180 presenters. The scientific poster program included 91 poster sessions, 2,115 posters, and 1,921 presenters. Grappling with overwhelm In sessions on supporting youth mental health, the impact of technology, and “adulthood unmoored,” APA speakers agreed that many of us are struggling to find purpose and optimism amid technological, climate, and global disruption. Psychologist Ali Mattu noted that over a decade ago, clients sought relief from stress and anxiety, which evolved to seeking relationship and connection support. “Now it’s despair, overwhelm, and meaning,” Mattu told the mainstage audience. “Anyone below the age of 50 here is really searching for meaning, connection, hope, and what do I do with all this overwhelm? What do I do with all of these systems that seem to be collapsing?” Perfectionism and the paradox of choice often lie at the root of the overwhelm, said Thomas Curran, associate professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics. “We don’t worry about what we are doing; we worry about what we could be doing,” Curran said. “It’s like swimming in a vast expanse of ocean with nowhere to dock. It’s frightening, and it feels like no matter what we do, it’s never enough.” The answer, Curran said: “Microdose bits of discomfort into daily life.” For young people, positive change means pushing back against the ubiquity of technology that purports to connect us but actually keeps us in separate bubbles, staring at our individual feeds. As Nikki Iyer, an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley, framed the problem: Our generation might be the most connected generation, but we’re also the loneliest generation. We’re the most alienated generation, and we are desperately craving social connection that we don’t know how to tap. . . . There’s so many people around you all the time. You’re on the train together; you’re in parks; you’re in cafes, but everyone is looking down, and that is a horrific way to grow up as social creatures. Iyer noted that tech firms wouldn’t be spending such unprecedented amounts of money on lobbying and marketing if they didn’t realize there’s a surge of resistance to artificial intelligence and social media dominating our lives. “The world is in our hands if we are willing to make the leap,” she said, noting a return to “weird” hobbies and in-person activity that replace digital time. “I see a lot of young people pushing back against that.” AI models were trained on disproportionately white male–oriented data sets, noted Brendesha Tynes, professor of education and psychology at the University of Southern California’s Rossier School of Education, in urging a slowdown in the adoption of AI. “Anti-Blackness is the default setting in AI,” Tynes said. Young people need skills “to identify, critique, and cope with the algorithmic bias in technologies that they might witness, and then also to eventually create better AI technologies that don’t have anti-Blackness bias.” Intentional connection and advocacy In sessions across the three days of the conference, researchers presented papers and models for identifying and building on resilience in marginalized communities, from LGBTQ+ youth and adults to disabled and racially marginalized people of all ages. Joshua Parmenter, an assistant professor at Arizona State University, presented a resistance-resilience model with sexual- and gender-diverse people of color, which involves both individually untangling messages that undermine your well-being and finding collective ways to reclaim power. Jules Soper, a researcher at the Oklahoma State University, offered an investigation of resistance strategies that trans and gender-diverse people use in states that are passing anti-trans legislation. Alvin Thomas, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, noted that anyone can play a positive role in supporting another member of the community. “I have zero kids, and yet I will still call myself a father. I have nephews; I have nieces; I have kids that I mentor from across the Caribbean and across the U.S.,” Thomas said. Clare M. Mehta, professor of psychology at Emmanuel College and visiting researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, encouraged everyone to look for ways to be a “villager” who reaches out to another person, and seeks out connection in third spaces. She continued: We have to start going back to the pub again. People have been concerned for years and years that drinking alcohol is bad for your health, but not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. . . . You don’t have to drink alcohol at the pub. They serve other drinks, right? Go and have a glass of orange juice or like a fizzy water. Not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. Young people actually are wired to be a positive force for change, said Eva Telzer, professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. “Young people are superhuman in the way their brains are set up to be risk takers but also to care about others, for peers, and for social interactions to be so important,” Telzer said in a question-and-answer period after her mainstage remarks. “That puts them in this perfect place to make change and do good in the world.” Even technology has a role to play, Mattu said. “AI should be a co-intelligence that enhances the things we are very bad at,” he said, urging people to take the opportunity to define clearly the uniquely human pursuits we should claim, and in which domains technology is appropriate to be a useful aid. He suggested three criteria for the activities to avoid replacing with AI: what you love, what you have expertise in, and what you hold high standards for. As Jacqueline S. Mattis, a psychologist and dean at Rutgers University, Newark, told her audience: We start as this passel of cells, and then we end up laughing, and that’s amazing. You get to experience the magnificence of being able to feel affection for another human being, so much so that you will sacrifice everything for them. That’s amazing. . . . All of that is what defines us as truly human and defines this thing called life as worth living.

Not sure what to get for the new grad heading to college or for your loved one who works from home? An Uplift desk gift card is a great way to help with these big purchases without making the weighty decision on someone else's behalf. Uplift gift cards are valid for five years from the purchase date and are available in increments from $50 to $5,000.

Uplift standing desks aren’t just for individuals; they’re also a great way to get the whole office healthier this year. #10231. Nvidia adds possible hack to list of very bad things under investigation

Ransomware group sets a deadline for the chipmaker to pay up - or see its data leaked

Finding a new CEO is just one of their problems. Nvidia is investigating an alleged breach following claims by ransomware group The Gentlemen's affiliates that they hacked the AI giant and stole sensitive information.

The embattled chipmaker told The Register's that it was investigating a possible third-party data breach. “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson said. “We continue to monitor the situation."

The ransomware gang’s data-leak site, shared on social media and seen by The Register, doesn’t show any stolen files or indicate what information the group claims to have stolen. Nvidia first appeared on the criminals’ blog on Wednesday, with The Gentlemen promising “DATA INFO - SOON.”

The post also included a countdown, ending November 28.

While we can’t verify the criminals’ claims, the group, which emerged in mid-2025, is one of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service operations. Its affiliates claimed more than 320 victims as of April, with the majority of these alleged ransomware infections (240) occurring in the first half of 2026.

The actual count, however, is likely much higher. Check Point researchers accessed an affiliate’s live command-and-control server during an incident response case earlier this year. The server contained victim telemetry that revealed more than 1,570 victims, mostly located in the US, and primarily corporate and organizational environments.

According to an operational technology (OT) threat report from Trellix published on Wednesday, industrial ransomware claims jumped nearly 51 percent - to about 1,500 posts- compared to last quarter, and The Gentlemen’s affiliates were the most prolific claim posters during this time period. They accounted for about 16 percent of all posts.

In February 2022, an Nvidia data breach exposed employees’ credentials and proprietary code. Extortion crew Lapsus$ claimed to be responsible for that intrusion and data theft.®
